sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities advanced as easing AI-valuation jitters and a late-week rebound lifted risk appetite, even amid record-high long-dated Treasury yields and Middle East oil volatility. MSCI World rose roughly **0.7%** (approx., verify before merging), with MSCI Developed Markets similar (approx., verify before merging) and MSCI Emerging Markets broadly flat near **1,709** (approx., verify before merging). In the US, the S&P 500 gained **1.15%** to a record **7,811.54**, the Dow added **0.93%** to **51,654.95** and the Nasdaq rose **0.64%** to **27,366.17**, with both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq setting fresh all-time highs as the MAG7 mega-cap tech cohort led. In Europe, the Euro Stoxx 50 eased around **1%** to roughly **6,170** (approx., verify before merging). In APAC, Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about **1.1%** to **69,030.92**, Hong Kong's Hang Seng rebounded roughly **1.0%** to **24,211.35**, and China's CSI 300 reopened from Golden Week near **4,317** (approx., verify before merging).

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities finished higher but choppy day to day, as AI-related volatility, Middle East developments and swings in energy prices and Treasury yields buffeted sentiment. The S&P 500 advanced **1.15%** to a record **7,811.54**, the Nasdaq Composite added **0.64%** to **27,366.17** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose **0.93%** to **51,654.95**, with both the S&P 500 and Nasdaq notching fresh all-time highs.

The dominant macro force remained the bond market: long-dated UST yields touched their highest levels since 2002 before pulling back, with the 10-year peaking near **5.35%** mid-week, pressuring valuations and stoking higher-for-longer fears. Oil added to the unease, with Brent briefly topping **USD 105** on reported Strait of Hormuz tanker attacks before easing after President Trump signalled restraint towards Iran.

Leadership tilted back to growth as AI jitters faded, with mega-cap tech and chip names pacing the advance into Friday's close ahead of the Q3 earnings season. Rate-sensitive and cyclical segments lagged, while a volatile HY market amid renewed inflation concerns kept broader risk appetite in check.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities were choppy and finished mixed, with the pan-regional STOXX Europe 600 whipsawing between an early-week rebound and a near four-month low before recovering into Friday. The Euro Stoxx 50 eased around **1%** on the week to roughly **6,170**, lagging a record-setting Wall Street.

The backdrop stayed dominated by surging global bond yields and renewed euro-area fiscal anxiety, with French politics and heavy corporate issuance lifting sovereign yields towards recent peaks. Banks bore the brunt, dropping nearly **2%** on Thursday to a three-month low as Deutsche Bank, Santander, Société Générale and UniCredit slid, while rising oil prices added to the pressure.

Investors parsed the ECB's latest meeting accounts for policy clues against still-elevated inflation, keeping the central bank's tone cautious. Dispersion was wide, with rate-sensitive financials and energy-exposed names lagging, before the index clawed back losses in a broad Friday bounce as yields steadied.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian equities were broadly firmer, led by Japan, where the Nikkei 225 rose about **1.1%** to **69,030.92** after surging **2.4%** to **69,946.40** on Monday — its highest close since July — on an AI-driven rally. Chip-related names paced gains, with Advantest up **4.5%** and Tokyo Electron adding **5.7%**, though the index drifted lower later in the week as high Treasury yields and oil prices tempered momentum ahead of earnings.

Chinese markets reopened after the Golden Week holiday to a shaky start, with the CSI 300 touching its lowest since August 2025 intraday before stabilising near **4,317**. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rebounded roughly **1.0%** to **24,211.35**, recouping part of the prior week's sharp technology-led slump.

The regional tone reflected the global AI-versus-rates tug-of-war: easing valuation jitters and resilient tech demand supported sentiment, even as multi-decade-high developed-market yields and firmer oil capped gains across higher-beta Asian growth names.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar stayed firm and near year-to-date highs, supported by hawkish Fed signals, US fiscal and oil-price risks, and the backup in Treasury yields, with Convera flagging that Fed, fiscal and oil risks remain supportive ahead of key US inflation data. The DXY held around the **102** level reached earlier in the cycle.

The euro extended its slide, declining for a fifth consecutive week as French fiscal and political concerns weighed; Convera described the currency as stretched but still vulnerable, with EUR/USD pinned near multi-month lows. Sterling was comparatively rangebound, though lingering risks remained as elevated global yields and UK-specific uncertainty limited any upside.

The yen stayed soft against a broadly stronger dollar as rate differentials remained wide, while higher developed-market yields and firmer oil pressured higher-beta emerging-market currencies, reinforcing the dollar's broad advance.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities headed for their first weekly gain in three, with Saxo noting all sectors higher as fuel tightness and resurgent gold demand supported a broad recovery. Geopolitics returned to the fore, with Middle East tensions and Strait of Hormuz risks lifting the energy complex.

Crude rallied on physical tightness rather than normalised supply, as tight distillate markets and high freight costs underpinned prices; Brent briefly topped **USD 105** intraday before paring gains as diplomatic signals towards Iran eased the risk premium. Refined products and natural gas reflected the same fuel-market stress.

Gold advanced, supported by steady ETF inflows, renewed Chinese buying and fiscal-health worries, holding firm even as real yields climbed to multi-year highs. Copper and industrial metals stayed historically elevated on Chinese demand and tight inventories, with speculative positioning near multi-year highs, underscoring persistent supply-side support across the complex.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign bonds were again the week's focal point as a global sell-off pushed long-dated yields to multi-decade highs before a partial retreat. The 10-year UST peaked near **5.35%** mid-week — its highest since 2002 — before settling around **5.25%**, with the 30-year near **5.61%** and the 2-year about **4.80%**; the largest increases were concentrated in shorter maturities.

Rate expectations swung as hawkish Fed commentary and firm data early in the week lifted yields, before markets pared the odds of an October hike to roughly **15–20%**, down from about **70%** a week earlier. Renewed inflation concerns and rising oil prices kept the higher-for-longer narrative alive.

Credit tone was mixed: the high-yield market turned volatile amid the inflation scare and energy swings, while investment-grade held comparatively steady. The late-week equity rebound and stabilising yields helped steady sentiment across IG and HY into Friday's close.
